key_insight: Introduce tensor similarity: a weight-space metric for tensor-based models that identifies when two modules implement the same computation by being invariant to weight-space symmetries. It enables comparison of internal mechanisms beyond behavior and basis-dependent parameters.
problem_solved: Existing similarity measures either rely on empirical behavior (failing to detect shared mechanisms out-of-distribution) or depend on specific parameter bases (ignoring symmetries); this work gives a symmetry-invariant, weight-based test for mechanistic equivalence of tensor modules.
method: Define a group-invariant distance/metric on weight tensors that factors out common tensor symmetries (e.g., permutations and modewise invertible/orthogonal transforms).

Align or compare tensor factors using decomposition and modewise alignment (efficient linear-algebra routines such as SVD/Procrustes or low-rank approximations) to compute a maximal similarity score under allowable symmetry transforms.
Validate the metric on representative tensor-based components to show it identifies equivalent mechanisms that behavioral or naive parameter comparisons miss.
impact: Provides a principled tool for mechanistic interpretability, enabling model developers and researchers to verify that two parts truly implement the same computation even across reparameterizations — useful for understanding, merging, and auditing models.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: empirical-behavior similarity vs tensor-similarity showing cases where behavior matches but mechanisms differ and vice versa.
Schematic of a weight tensor with modewise transforms and an arrow to an aligned tensor (visualizing the symmetry-invariant alignment step).
Heatmap or matrix of pairwise tensor-similarity scores across modules, highlighting clusters of equivalent mechanisms.
Flowchart of the pipeline: input weight tensors → decomposition/alignment → compute invariant similarity → decision/visualization.
paper_title: When Are Two Networks the Same? Tensor Similarity for Mechanistic Interpretability
paper_authors: ML Nissen Gonzalez, Melwina Albuquerque, Laurence Wroe, Jacob Meyer Cohen, Logan Riggs Smith
